ozet: From the barren valley where Abraham settled his family to the trading town of Quraysh: the building of the Ka'ba, the coming of idol worship and the Mecca of Qusayy.

b01-s01: Mecca lies in a valley surrounded by mountains.
The land around it is dry, almost a desert, with little vegetation. The Qur'an calls it «an uncultivable valley».
This episode is the story of that valley and of the house at its centre.
b01-s02: Long ago, the Prophet Abraham brought his wife Hagar and his young son Ishmael to this empty valley.
The Qur'an records his prayer: «Our Lord! Indeed, I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near Your holy House, our Lord! that they may establish proper worship.»
b01-s03: Thanks to the water of Zamzam, life began in this barren valley.
The Yemeni tribe of Jurhum settled in the valley with Hagar's permission.
Ishmael grew up among them and learned Arabic from them; he married into Jurhum and became kin to the tribe.
b01-s04: Years later, Abraham came to visit his son.
Together they raised the foundations of the Ka'ba.
The Qur'an tells of that moment through their prayer: «Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Indeed, You, only You, are the Hearer, the Knower.»
b01-s05: After Abraham, for a long time the Ka'ba was visited only for the worship of Allah.
But in time the people of Jurhum strayed from that path.
Then the tribe of Khuza'a, together with the tribe of Kinana, defeated Jurhum and took control of Mecca.
b01-s06: When 'Amr ibn Luhayy of Khuza'a took charge of Mecca and the Ka'ba, he corrupted the belief in one God and spread idol worship.
According to the reports, he was the first to change the religion of Ishmael and to set up idols.
b01-s07: Quraysh, the tribe of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), had long lived outside Mecca, scattered.
In the fifth century, Qusayy ibn Kilab of Quraysh fought against Khuza'a with the help of the tribes of Kinana and Quda'a.
After the fighting, the two sides turned to an arbiter. He ruled that Qusayy had the better right to the Ka'ba and to Mecca.
So the rule of Mecca and the Ka'ba passed to Quraysh.
b01-s08: Qusayy settled the scattered clans of Quraysh around the Ka'ba and divided Mecca among the branches of the tribe.
In this way Quraysh moved from a half-nomadic life to a settled one.
To the north of the Ka'ba, Qusayy built a council house whose door opened onto the Ka'ba: Dar al-Nadwa.
Important matters such as war, peace and marriage were discussed there. The sons of Qusayy and clan chiefs over forty years of age could take part in the council.
b01-s09: Qusayy also held the honoured duties of guarding the Ka'ba, providing water and food for the pilgrims, and carrying the banner.
After him these duties passed to his eldest son, 'Abd al-Dar. When the sons of 'Abd Manaf also claimed them, the branches of Quraysh formed two rival alliances.
The two sides came to the brink of fighting. In the end those who favoured agreement prevailed, and the duties were divided between the two families.
b01-s10: In time, idols were set up inside and around the Ka'ba; it is reported that by the time of Quraysh they numbered three hundred and sixty.
The greatest of them was Hubal.
Even so, the Meccans never dedicated the Ka'ba to any idol; they always regarded it as the House of Allah.
The Hanifs, who held to the religion of Abraham, kept away from the idols and continued to visit the Ka'ba.
b01-s11: The soil of Mecca was not fit for farming; Quraysh lived by trade.
Because the area around the Ka'ba was held inviolable, people could come to Mecca without fear, and this made the town's trade grow.
Hashim, the Prophet's great-grandfather, and his brothers made agreements with neighbouring states and with the tribes along the roads.
So the caravans of Quraysh began to travel safely to Yemen and Abyssinia in winter, and to Syria and Anatolia in summer.

The Qur'an mentions these journeys: «For the taming of Qureysh, for their taming (We cause) the caravans to set forth in winter and summer. So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and has made them safe from fear.»
b01-s12: In Arab tribal society, especially among the desert Bedouin, what bound people together was blood.
Everyone sided blindly with their own tribe; a crime was held against the tribe rather than the person, and blood feuds went on and on.
Someone who left their tribe could take refuge with another tribe through an agreement, or become its ally.

Years later Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, who had become a Muslim, would describe those days to the ruler of Abyssinia: they had worshipped idols, cut the ties of kinship, wronged their neighbours, and the strong had crushed the weak.
b01-s13: Years later the Messenger of Allah would say: «The best of people in the time of Ignorance are the best of them in Islam.»
The leader of the sons of Hashim in this Mecca was 'Abd al-Muttalib, son of Hashim. Quraysh sought his opinion in their disputes.
He had reopened the well of Zamzam, which the people of Jurhum had filled in and left unmarked; the duty of providing water and food for the pilgrims was also his.
